segments.text: Welcome to RoboDaily, your daily dose of the latest news from the world of robotics.
August 14th, 2026.
Today we're diving into satellite repairs, Sony's latest robotic hand innovations, and what the future holds for mobile manipulators and humanoids.
Join us as we explore it all.
From Robotics & Automation News, "Northrop Grumman launches robotic spacecraft to repair and extend life of satellites."
Northrop Grumman has successfully launched the Mission Robotic Vehicle (MRV), a groundbreaking robotic spacecraft designed to service satellites in orbit.

The MRV features two fully articulated robotic arms capable of manipulating specialized tools during servicing operations, allowing it to perform tasks such as satellite inspection, relocation, repair, upgrades, debris removal, and robotic assembly.

The spacecraft itself boasts a passive refueling module and computing hardware intended to support future AI-powered operations, including the installation of propulsion modules on existing satellites, thereby extending their lifespan without necessitating replacement.
From Robotics & Automation News, "Sony robot hand patent hints at renewed interest in humanoid robotics".
Sony has filed a US patent application that outlines its research into a robotic hand featuring a human-like opposable thumb.
The patent, published by the US Patent and Trademark Office on August 6, describes a robot hand designed to reproduce the movements of the human thumb for manipulating objects.
The design focuses on the mechanical aspect of the hand mechanism, which breaks movement into three separate rotation points to enable opposition between the thumb and fingers.
This allows for more precise control over grasping and releasing objects.
The application has significant implications beyond humanoid robots, with potential applications in service robots, remotely operated machines, and systems utilizing tools designed for humans.
This development suggests that Sony is re-examining its approach to humanoid robotics, a field that has seen significant advancements in recent years.
As the company continues to develop this technology, it may lead to innovative solutions for various industries and applications.
From The Robot Report, "Mobile manipulators and humanoids: The future of robotics"
, a growing field in robotics has emerged with mobile manipulators and humanoids being deployed in factories and warehouses.

Industry experts discussed technical concerns such as power management, perception, and data collection for AI and world models, sharing lessons learned from scaling advanced systems from the automotive industry.
Lattice Semiconductor emphasized the need for reliability and security in AI-enabled humanoid robots, particularly those used in public-facing applications.

Researchers are exploring human-machine interaction and skills training for humanoid service robots, with panelists highlighting the importance of these advancements to enhance user experience and efficiency.
From Robotics & Automation News, "Geekplus launches RoboShuttle Hyper for high-throughput warehouse fulfillment"

, Geekplus has unveiled its latest innovation in warehouse automation, specifically the RoboShuttle Hyper, a next-generation tote-to-person climbing Autonomous Mobile Robot (AMR) solution designed to enhance high-throughput warehouse fulfillment.

The system achieves impressive efficiency rates by delivering up to 6,000 totes per hour per 1,000 square meters and features advanced parallel horizontal and vertical climbing capabilities, resulting in 50% higher concurrency compared to the industry standard.
Additionally, the RoboShuttle Hyper supports dual-robot operation within the same column and boasts a column-rail-integrated system for improved reliability and overall performance.
From Robotics & Automation News, "Schaeffler unveils formed strain wave gearboxes for humanoid robots".

Schaeffler has introduced a groundbreaking innovation in the humanoid robotics market by developing formed strain wave gearboxes, which are key components of actuators that represent around half of the manufacturing costs of humanoid robots.
The company's innovative forming technology enables the production of these critical components in mere seconds, significantly reducing production time and material consumption by over 75%.
This breakthrough method achieves comparable torques and efficiencies to conventionally manufactured components while maintaining high dimensional accuracy and process stability.
Production of these gearboxes will commence in Germany in 2027, with plans to expand to other regions in the coming years.
From Robotics & Automation News, "LG to unveil new Nvidia-powered humanoid robot in early 2027."
LG is developing a next-generation bipedal humanoid robot that will be unveiled in the first quarter of 2027.
The robot's development involves collaboration with Nvidia, utilizing the Isaac GR00T platform for advanced reasoning and Nvidia Jetson Thor for onboard compute.

This partnership will enable the creation of more sophisticated robots, such as wheel-based models like CLOiD, designed to operate in various environments including manufacturing facilities, homes, and commercial spaces.
These robots are expected to be deployed across LG's global production lines.
From Planet ROS, "ROS Discourse General: Launching the VLAs on the Humanoid robot(G1, T800) for continues tasks."
Currently, a key hurdle in successfully integrating Visual Lenses (VLAs) on the Humanoid robot G1 (T800) for continuous tasks is being encountered due to the realsense pack of cameras.
In particular, the implementation of the unifolm VLA requires multiple cameras, necessitating two cameras on wrists and two on shoulders.
Despite these challenges, researchers have made progress in overcoming this limitation by developing alternative camera configurations that can accommodate the specific requirements of various VLAs.
These findings are expected to enable more efficient and effective use of VLAs on humanoid robots like G1 (T800) for tasks such as object recognition and manipulation.
The development of these new camera configurations involved a thorough analysis of the realsense pack's capabilities and limitations, as well as the specific needs of various VLAs.
By identifying potential workarounds and optimizing camera placement, researchers were able to successfully deploy VLAs on G1 (T800) for continuous tasks.
The successful deployment demonstrates the feasibility of using VLAs in humanoid robots, which could have significant implications for fields such as robotics and computer vision.

The findings from this research are likely to be widely adopted in the AI and tech industry, enabling the development of more advanced robotic systems that can perform complex tasks with greater accuracy and efficiency.
As a result, researchers and engineers should watch for further advancements in humanoid robot technology and the integration of VLAs into these systems.
From Robotics & Automation News, "Robot.com unveils R-dog quadruped robot for last-mile delivery and advertising."

Robot.com has unveiled its latest innovation, R-dog, a four-legged delivery robot designed to navigate the last 100 meters of deliveries in areas with obstacles such as stairs, curbs, and uneven ground.
The robot can carry large payloads and features an onboard compartment that can hold multiple items at once, making it ideal for fast and efficient delivery services.

Additionally, R-dog's second application is interactive advertising through R-ads, which allows brands to remotely upload and manage campaigns on the robot's dual video screens, providing a new and engaging way for businesses to reach their target audience.
From Robotics & Automation News, "AutoStore signs global supply agreement with Amazon."

AutoStore has established a global supply agreement with Amazon, which sets forth terms for future procurement of its automation systems without committing the retailer to purchasing any particular quantity of equipment.
The deal creates an established framework for future installations without requiring negotiation on underlying terms for each procurement.

Approximately 2,000 of its systems are currently installed across 68 countries, focusing on "Intelligent Fulfillment" that combines automation, software, and AI to manage and optimize fulfillment operations.
This agreement is seen as a significant development in the expansion of AutoStore's global presence.
The specifics of the agreement were not disclosed, with no mention of potential order volumes or financial terms.

However, AutoStore has stated that this deal will provide a consistent framework for future installations, streamlining the procurement process and reducing reliance on negotiations on each individual sale.
The company's existing installed base in 68 countries serves as a strong foundation for this partnership.
The global supply agreement with Amazon is expected to further solidify AutoStore's position in the market, particularly in the realm of automation and AI-driven logistics solutions.
As the demand for efficient fulfillment operations continues to grow, companies like AutoStore are poised to capitalize on emerging trends in robotics and technology.
From Humanoids Daily, "The Great Dexterity Divide: Why Robotics Leaders Are Warring Over Tendon vs. Direct-Drive Hands."
Companies like 1X and Tesla are investing in tendon-driven hands for compliance, while Sharpa and Wuji Tech favor direct-drive motors with high precision.

The debate centers around the engineering and design choices made by these companies, particularly Figure's early tendon-driven hand design, which was criticized by CEO Brett Adcock as an "engineering mistake."
However, Foundation engineer Andrea Esposito countered that the issue lies in a "skills issue" related to poor routing and weak actuation.
This disparity highlights the ongoing struggle to develop a truly general-purpose humanoid robot with a reliable and effective hand, a key challenge in the field of robotics.
From Robohub, "What does it take for a robot to hold a conversation with a room, not just a person?"
This story explores the challenges of enabling robots to engage in simultaneous conversations with multiple individuals and highlights the complexity of multi-party human-robot interaction.

Researchers and industry professionals at the Imperial Robotics Summer School, hosted at Imperial College, London, have been working on developing robots that can hold conversations with rooms, not just people.
They achieved this by exploring various challenges, including detecting active speakers in real time and tracking individuals through interactions.
The group focused on enabling robots to generate natural gaze behavior, a crucial aspect of human communication.
Through interdisciplinary research, the project shed light on the importance of considering multiple factors when designing multi-party human-robot interaction systems.
